Predicting Nonadherence to Mobile Health Interventions 
 
Planned Publication: Jakob R, Benning L, Sévin CM, Von Wangenheim F, Fleisch E, Kowatsch 
T. Predicting Nonadherence to Mobile Health Interventions. In: (2025) (In preparation) 
 
Abstract 
 
The rising prevalence and economic burden of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) present a 
significant challenge to patients and healthcare systems, calling for innovative, scalable, and cost-
effective solutions. Mobile health (mHealth) interventions, facilitated by the ubiquity of 
smartphones, have emerged as promising tools to support the prevention and management of NCDs. 
Yet, despite growing evidence and availability, mHealth interventions face high nonadherence, 
where users fail to use these tools as intended or discontinue use entirely before achieving desired 
outcomes. The rich data collected by mHealth interventions raise the question of whether – and to 
what extent – nonadherence can be predicted using these data. If so, such predictions could inform 
targeted strategies aimed at preventing nonadherence before it fully manifests. We developed 
machine learning models for the prediction of nonadherence in two mHealth interventions, one for 
nonspecific and degenerative back pain over a program duration of 90 days (Vivira, n = 8,372), and 
another for hypertension self-management over 186 days (Manoa, n = 6,674). Our models identified 
an average of 94% of nonadherent users between Weeks 2 and 13 in Vivira (mean AUC = 0.95), 
defined as completing fewer than eight therapeutic exercises per week. In Manoa, our models 
correctly identified an average of 86% of nonadherent users between months 2 and 6 (mean AUC 
= 0.82), defined as completing fewer than one blood pressure measurement week per month. 
Additionally, models predicting churn (users’ last login within program duration) achieved mean 
AUCs of 0.87 for both apps, correctly identifying 84-86% of churned users. These findings 
demonstrate that nonadherence can be accurately predicted, highlighting a unique and underutilized 
advantage of mHealth interventions – the ability to transform app engagement data into actionable 
insights that may inform targeted strategies to promote adherence.

1 Introduction 
Digital health interventions (DHIs) have demonstrated the potential to assist patients and healthcare 
systems in addressing the global rise and financial impact of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), 
which are the leading causes of death and disability worldwide [16, 26, 44, 64]. In particular, mobile 
health (mHealth) interventions have emerged as versatile tools to promote behavior change among 
patients, improve health outcomes, and reduce healthcare costs due to the widespread availability 
of smartphones [8, 38, 49, 60]. A growing body of evidence suggests that mHealth interventions 
can effectively support the prevention and management of NCDs by addressing modifiable risk 
factors, including physical inactivity [52, 53], unhealthy diets [67], tobacco use [63], the harmful 
use of alcohol [12] and metabolic risk factors such as obesity [52], hypertension [1], and 
hyperglycemia [19]. Furthermore, mHealth interventions show promise in improving mental health 
conditions, including depression and anxiety [10, 31]. In light of this, first healthcare systems with 
population-wide coverage now include mHealth interventions as reimbursable items in patient 
coverage, and prescriptions for mHealth interventions are starting to become a more common part 
of treatment plans and health insurance benefits packages [13, 25, 48, 58]. In Germany, for example, 
mHealth interventions have been introduced as prescription digital therapies (PDT) to the 
collectively funded statutory health insurance (SHI) system with scalable reimbursement strategies 
under the German Digital Healthcare Act in 2019 [46]. While the SHI system provides coverage 
for approximately 90% of the German population, a private health insurance (PHI) system covers 
the remaining proportion of the coverage to meet the legal requirement of universal health insurance 
coverage of the German population [4]. Similar to the SHI system, the PHI system is exploring 
options of digital care and is expanding its spectrum of PDT solutions. 
However, despite the increasing availability and demonstrated efficacy of mHealth interventions, a 
substantial proportion of users fail to adhere to these programs as intended or disengage 
prematurely, posing a major barrier to their effectiveness [9, 18]. Although the specific metrics used 
to quantify adherence vary across DHI studies, there is broad consensus that adherence is 
suboptimal. A systematic review focusing on mHealth interventions for chronic diseases (17 
studies) reported a pooled dropout rate of 43%, with observational studies exhibiting a higher rate 
(49%) compared to more controlled randomized controlled trials (40%) [34]. Another review of 83 
web-based interventions concluded that only half of users adhered to the interventions [24]. A study 
evaluating user engagement with 59 mental health apps found that fewer than 10% of users logged 
in daily after seven days, and by Day 15, the median open rate had declined to 3.9% [2]. Additional 
research corroborates these findings, with up to 80% of users of mHealth interventions engaging 
only at a minimal level, logging into mHealth apps no more than once, and failing to use the apps 
consistently over extended periods [11, 34, 43]. 

 
3 
The growing body of literature on mHealth interventions also highlights the need for more rigorous 
approaches to measuring adherence to DHIs. Sieverink et al. (2017) noted that adherence remains 
an underdeveloped and often improperly utilized concept in the existing literature [50]. Their 
review of 62 studies revealed that 34 studies operationalized adherence as “the more use, the better,” 
while only 28 studies established a clear threshold for the intended use of the technology. To 
enhance the comparability and reliability of adherence measurements, they proposed that future 
studies should define adherence based on a specific threshold aligned with the technology’s 
intended use, also ensuring that this intended use is clearly defined and justified [50]. This definition 
distinguishes nonadherence from the concept of churn – also referred to as dropout, abandonment, 
or attrition – which is considered a key indicator for the adoption and success of mobile applications 
[17, 35]. Churn refers to a user discontinuing use of a mobile application entirely and is thus closely 
related to nonadherence and can be viewed as a severe form of nonadherence. 
While the prediction of nonadherence in accordance with the definition of Sieverink et al. (2017) 
constitutes a research gap, a growing body of research suggests that churn in mHealth interventions 
can be accurately predicted based on behavioral app engagement data (e.g., app login or session 
counts) [5, 14, 30, 37, 40, 57]. However, existing studies have predicted churn only at specific 
points in time, leaving limited evidence on prediction performances at different stages of the user 
journey. Likewise, it is unclear to what extent prediction models can predict churn before users 
fully disengage. Addressing this research gap, Jakob et al. (2024) recently predicted churn at the 
end of each day of users’ initial week of usage in a public digital weight loss intervention, also 
testing a wide range of features and ML algorithms. The best-performing model in this study was a 
random forest model that only used daily login counts, achieving an F1 score of 0.87 (AUC = 0.73, 
Accuracy = 81%) on Day 7 and an average F1 score of 0.84 over the initial week (mean AUC = 
0.71, mean Accuracy = 0.76). Churn prediction models in this study improved in terms of F1, AUC, 
and Accuracy from Day 1 to Day 7, hinting at a progressive improvement in churn prediction over 
time. Notably, the study also analyzed the number of users who reengaged with the app after a 
correct churn prediction to assess the potential of in-app interventions to prevent churn. The best-
performing model correctly predicted an average of 93% of churned users over the initial week with 
a mean false positive rate of 58.7%, and correctly predicted 81% of churned users who would 
reengage after a correct churn prediction. These findings suggest that prediction models may not 
only serve as early detection tools but can provide actionable insights for the delivery of targeted 
strategies to promote adherence before users fully disengage. However, the study also noted a 
shortcoming regarding a restricted focus on the initial week of app usage, calling for further studies 
in diverse settings with extended observation windows to assess how the predictive performance 
and the potential for mitigation strategies evolve over extended periods [21]. 

 4 
This study addresses this research gap by evaluating nonadherence prediction models in two distinct 
mHealth interventions (Vivira and Manoa) across different regulatory environments (i.e. SHI and 
PHI), medical conditions addressed (i.e. nonspecific back pain and arterial hypertension), program 
durations (i.e. 90 and 186 days), user demographics, as well as different therapeutic approaches (i.e. 
guided movement therapy and personalized hypertension self-management). To provide a 
comprehensive perspective, we predict nonadherence relative to the intended use of the 
interventions, following the definition by Sieverink et al. (2017), as well as its most severe form: 
churn (i.e., complete discontinuation). Building on Jakob et al. (2024), we also examine the 
proportion of users who reengage after a correct prediction, offering insights into the potential for 
targeted strategies to promote adherence before churn occurs. Through these analyses, we aim to 
determine the extent to which nonadherence to mHealth interventions can be predicted. 
2 Methods 
2.1 Datasets and Definitions of Nonadherence 
2.1.1 Vivira 
The first anonymized dataset was collected from “Vivira”, a CE-marked Medical Device 
Regulation risk class I mHealth intervention for nonspecific and degenerative backpain which is 
approved as a “Digitale Gesundheitsanwendung” (DiGA) in the regulatory environment for PDTs 
in the German SHI system [46]. As a DiGA, the medical effectiveness of Vivira was confirmed by 
the German Federal Institute for Medicines and Medical Devices (Bundesinstitut für Arzneimittel 
und Medizinprodukte, BfArM) , a regulatory body, based on a confirmatory study [61]. Further 
research supports the real-world effectiveness of Vivira [54, 55]. Under DiGA regulations, Vivira 
is available to all patients covered by the SHI system, but only accessible upon prescription by a 
qualified healthcare professional or upon a patient providing proof of medical need to their 
respective health insurance. A DiGA prescription for Vivira allows full access to the respective 
DiGA for 90 days. The Vivira app provides individualized and guided exercises for asynchronous 
and decentralized movement therapy. Educational content (e.g., exercise introductions, annotated 
video cues, information on the medical condition, and therapy principles) and behavioral cues (e.g., 
visualizations of therapy progress, reminders) prompt patients to interact with the app and support 
retention. The program aims to improve pain, mobility, strength, and coordination. Vivira is 
available for iOS and Android devices. 
The use of DiGA data is strictly limited. Therefore, only users who provided consent under Article 
4, Section 2, 4 of the DiGA regulations (DiGA-Verordnung, DiGAV) were included. The dataset 
included data from 8,372 users who activated their first prescription between January 1, 2023, and 
March 31, 2024. Of the included users who provided information on their gender (98%, 
8,208/8,372), 68.3% were female, 31.6% were male, and 0.1% non-binary. Among users who

provided information on their age range (99%, 8,251/8,372), 25% were aged 18–35 years, 23% 
were 36–45 years, 24% were 46–55 years, 21.1% were 56–65 years, 6.4% were 66–75 years, and 
1% were over 75 years old. 
For each user, binary daily activity data (active or inactive) was available based on whether the user 
triggered any app event on any day during their first 90-day prescription period. The dataset also 
included the number of exercises completed by each user on each day during the 90-day prescription 
period.  
The intended use of Vivira involves completing weekly exercises. The instruction for use 
recommends at least three sessions per week, each consisting of four independent exercises with 
accompanying audiovisual instructions and guidance. Yet, using a propensity score matching 
approach, Klingenberg et al. (2023) illustrated that a significantly higher probability of achieving a 
clinically meaningful improvement of pain intensity by the time of churn is already achieved by 
users who complete at least two sessions per week [28]. We therefore deem a minimum exercise 
frequency of two sessions (i.e. eight exercises) per week the minimum adherence to yield clinically 
relevant therapeutic benefits from the use of Vivira. Therefore, adherence was measured weekly, 
defined as completing eight or more exercises per week. Users with fewer than eight exercises per 
week were considered nonadherent. 
2.1.2 Manoa 
The second anonymized dataset was collected from "Manoa," a mHealth intervention designed for 
hypertension self-management. The Manoa app features a conversational agent (CA; a chatbot 
simulating conversation with human users) that collects user data and provides guidance on various 
health aspects, including lifestyle choices and medication adherence. Manoa is accessible to 
customers of seven of the ten largest private health insurance companies in the German and two of 
the ten largest in the Swiss PHI system. Manoa is available to individuals diagnosed with 
hypertension. Participating health insurance companies provide interested users with access codes 
for full six-month access. The app's core feature is a blood pressure diary. The CA offers 
personalized feedback on blood pressure levels based on a structured home blood pressure 
monitoring protocol, which has been associated with a reduction in average blood pressure and 
improvement in blood pressure control [3]. The app recommends scheduling a doctor's appointment 
if blood pressure levels are elevated. Users can share their blood pressure report digitally with their 
doctor or export it as a PDF. Manoa promotes regular monitoring through reminders, tracking, and 
motivational messages from the CA. Blood pressure data can be entered manually, scanned using 
the smartphone's camera, or imported directly from compatible measurement devices. Users are 
prompted to measure their blood pressure twice daily for six days during each home blood pressure 
monitoring period. Manoa is available for iOS and Android devices. 

 6 
The dataset included data from a total of 6,674 users. Of the included users who provided 
information on their gender (82.8%; 5,523/6,674), 21.7% were female and 78.3% were male. 
Among users who provided information on their age range (83.1%; 5,548/6,674), 0.9% were aged 
18–29 years, 6.1% were 30–44 years, 16.8% were 45–54 years, 34% were 55–64 years, 32.8% were 
65–74 years, and 9.4% were 75 years or older. 
For each user, the number of daily app sessions (continuous) during the 186-day program duration 
was available from which binary daily activity data (active or inactive) could be derived. 
The intended use of Manoa aligns with medical guidelines from the European Society of 
Hypertension (ESH) and European Society of Cardiology (ESC), recommending blood pressure 
measurements for 3-6 days once a month. After the initial period in the first month, the app sends 
periodic reminders every four weeks to continue monitoring with users being able adjust the timing 
of their home blood pressure monitoring periods. Adherence was measured monthly from months 
2 to 6 after the initial period, defined as completing at least one measurement week per month 
consisting of at least 3 within 7 days with morning and evening measurements. Users who did not 
complete a measurement week per month were considered nonadherent. 
2.2 Feature Selection, Model Training, and Evaluation 
Aligning with previous churn prediction studies that achieved accurate prediction results with daily 
behavioral app engagement features in the initial week of usage in DHIs for weight loss and 
smoking cessation [5, 21], we selected generalizable daily app engagement features related to users' 
activity and progress with the DHIs in this study. This choice is also consistent with churn 
prediction studies in other app domains, which have ranked features related to user app activity 
(e.g., daily logins) and app progress (e.g., completion of app-logged activities) as the most 
important features [7, 27, 29, 41, 56]. 
In Vivira, we predicted nonadherence weekly from Weeks 2 to 13 based on users’ daily app activity 
variables (active or inactive) and the daily number of completed exercises variables (continuous) 
of the preceding weeks. To illustrate this with an example, for the prediction of nonadherence in 
Week 2 (a user completing fewer than 8 exercises between Days 8 to 14), we utilized users’ daily 
app activity variables from Days 1 until 7 and the daily number of completed exercises from Days 
1 until 7. 
In Manoa, we predicted nonadherence monthly from Months 2 to 6 based on users’ daily app 
activity variables (active or inactive) and the number of daily app sessions (continuous) of the 
preceding months. To illustrate this with an example, for the prediction of nonadherence in Month 
2 (a user completing no measurement week between Days 32 to 63), we utilized users’ daily app 
activity variables from Days 1 until 31 and the number of daily app sessions from Days 1 until 31. 

 
7 
Additionally, we predicted churn (users’ last login within program duration) daily in Vivira (at the 
end of Days 1 to 82) and Manoa (at the end of Days 1 until 178) with a 7-Day prediction window 
based on features from previous days. To illustrate this with an example, for the prediction of churn 
at the end of Day 14, we predicted if the users’ last login occurs until the end of Day 21 based on 
input features from Days 1 until 14. The choice of a 7-day prediction window was based on the 
DHIs’ intended weekly use and seven days of inactivity, which are commonly used to define churn 
in other churn prediction studies [7, 23, 33, 36, 57, 62, 65]. 
Consistent with the aforementioned study by Jakob et al. (2024), we applied random forest 
algorithms for all predictions [21]. This choice is further supported by prediction studies in other 
app domains that achieved superior performance with random forest models across multiple tested 
ML algorithms [14, 21, 39, 45, 59]. We preprocessed available features by normalizing numerical 
data by performing square root scaling for right-skewed data and standard scaling for non-right-
skewed data. For nonadherence prediction in Vivira and churn prediction in both mHealth 
interventions, we randomly split 80% of the dataset into a training set (Vivira = 6,697, Manoa = 
5,339) and the remaining 20% into a test set (Vivira = 1,675, Manoa = 1,335). For nonadherence 
prediction in Manoa, we only included users who completed the initial blood pressure measurement 
week (n = 2,095), resulting in 1,676 users in the training set and 419 users in the test set. 
 We applied stratified 10-fold cross-validation and randomized search for hyperparameter tuning 
on the training sets, optimizing for F1 score for all models. Additionally, we applied Tomek Links 
undersampling to the training data to address class imbalance class before cross-validation [15]. 
Detailed hyperparameter grids are provided in Appendix 6.1. 
We evaluated model performance using F1 score, area under the curve (AUC), accuracy, precision, 
and recall. We also conducted feature importance analyses for each model to compare which 
features contribute the most to their predictive performance. 
To assess the intervention potential, we further categorized and distinguished between “churned 
users” (last login before prediction window), “churning users” (last login within prediction 
window), and “active users” (last login after prediction window). To illustrate this with an example, 
for a prediction at the end of Day 7 for the prediction window between Days 8 and 14, a user with 
a last login on Day 6 is considered “churned”, a user with a last login on Day 12 is considered 
“churning”, and a user with a last login on day 15 is considered “active”. 
We used freely available Python packages listed in Appendix 6.1 for data manipulation, analysis, 
modeling, and evaluation.

3 Results 
3.1 Descriptive Results 
3.1.1 Vivira 
Vivira users were active on an average of 15.5 days (SD = 19.6) and completed an average of 55.6 
exercises (SD = 76.5) during the 90-day program duration. The mean last day of logging into the 
app across all users was 38.5 (SD = 31.7). On a weekly basis, users were active for an average of 
4.9 weeks (SD = 4.0) and adherent for an average of 3.1 weeks (SD = 3.9) throughout the 
observation period. The mean number of weekly active days decreased from 3.1 (SD = 2.0) in Week 
1 to 0.4 (SD = 1.2) in Week 13, while the mean number of completed exercises decreased from 9.7 
(SD = 9.2) in Week 1 to 1.4 (SD = 4.4) in Week 13, indicating a progressive decrease in user 
engagement over time. Detailed descriptive statistics are provided in Appendix Tables 6.5 to 6.7. 
As highlighted in Figure 6.1, user churn was most severe at the beginning of the program with 
approximately 25% of users recording their last login during the first week and 8.8% in the second 
week. From Week 3 through Week 12, the relative churn rate remained relatively stable, within 
4.2% to 6.5% of users logging their last activity in each respective week until Week 13, in which 
13.2% of users remained active and thus recorded their last login in the final week.

3.1.2 Manoa

to accurately identify nonadherent users. 
Between Weeks 2 and 13, the models correctly identified an average of 98.3% (SD = 2.9%) of 
churned nonadherent users (those whose last login occurred before the 7-day prediction window), 
an average of 82.6% (SD = 7.1%) of churning nonadherent users (those whose last login occurred 
within the 7-day prediction window), and an average of 83.4% (SD = 3.4%) of active nonadherent 
users (those whose last login occurred after the 7-day prediction window), with a mean false 
positive rate of 24.2% (SD = 2.9%). This indicates that the models were more adept at identifying 
nonadherent users who had already churned than those active or in the process of churning, as 
highlighted in Figure 6.5. Overall, nonadherence prediction models identified an average of 94.2% 
(SD = 4.2%) of total nonadherent users from Week 2 to Week 13. 
A detailed evaluation of feature importances across all prediction models can be found in Appendix 
6.2. The evaluation revealed that daily exercise features (mean cumulated feature importance = 
0.59) were more important for nonadherence prediction models than daily activity features (mean 
cumulated feature importance = 0.41) in each individual week. The importance of both activity and 
exercise features tended to increase with their proximity to the prediction window (See Appendix 
6.2).

Monthly nonadherence prediction results in Manoa are presented in Table 6.3, and Figure 6.7 
further illustrates prediction performance trends for the prediction windows from Month 2 until 
Month 6. 
AUC of prediction models increased from 0.73 in Month 2 to 0.86 in Month 4 and slightly decreased 
afterward to 0.85 in Month 6. Accuracy improved from 0.70 in Week 2 to 0.81 in Month 5. In 
Month 6, accuracy equaled the class imbalance (0.81) thus offering limited utility. F1-score 
increased across months, ranging from 0.73 in Month 2 to 0.89 in Month 6. Precision and recall 
also gradually increased, with precision varying between 0.72 and 0.86 and recall ranging from 
0.73 to 0.93.  
Across the prediction windows from Month 2 to Month 6, the models achieved a mean AUC of 
0.82 (SD = 0.06), a mean accuracy of 0.77 (SD = 0.05), a mean F1-score of 0.83 (SD = 0.07), a 
mean precision of 0.81 (SD = 0.06), and a mean recall of 0.86 (SD = 0.08). 
Between Months 2 and 6, the models correctly identified an average of 97.1% (SD = 2.8%) of 
churned nonadherent users (those whose last login occurred before the 31-day prediction window), 
an average of 92.6% (SD = 5.2%) of churning nonadherent users (those whose last login occurred 
within the 31-day prediction window), and an average of 74.9% (SD = 4.3%) of active nonadherent 
users (those whose last login occurred after the 31-day prediction window), with a mean false 
positive rate (FPR) of 49.5% (SD = 12.9%). These results highlight that the models were more 
adept at identifying nonadherent users who had already churned rather than those active or in the 
process of churning, as highlighted in Figure 6.7. Overall, nonadherence prediction models 
identified an average of 85.9% (SD = 7.6%) of total nonadherent users from Month 2 to Month 6. 
The feature importance analyses showed that daily session features (mean cumulated feature 
importance = 0.73) were more important for nonadherence prediction models than daily activity 
features (mean cumulated feature importance = 0.27). The importance of both session and activity 
features tended to increase with their proximity to the prediction window (See Appendix 6.2).

4 Discussion 
4.1 Predicting Nonadherence to Mobile Health Interventions 
Our findings show that nonadherence to mHealth interventions can be accurately predicted over 
extended program durations, both in terms of adherence relative to intended use as defined by 
Sieverink et al. (2017) and in its most severe form – churn (i.e., complete discontinuation of use). 
Our study thus extends prior research showing that methodologies effective in predicting churn 
during the first week [21], remain applicable over longer durations of 90 and 186 days across two 
distinct mHealth interventions to predict nonadherence. Given the conceptual link between churn 
and nonadherence – where fully disengaged users are inherently nonadherent – these results are 
intuitive. Our descriptive analysis further emphasizes this relationship, showing that the decline in 
adherence over time in Vivira and Manoa is largely driven by churn (i.e. users discontinuing 
entirely). 
Weekly nonadherence prediction models in Vivira achieved strong performance, correctly 
identifying an average of 94.2% (SD = 4.2%, mean AUC = 0.95) of nonadherent users between 
Weeks 2 and 13, with an average false positive rate of 24.2% (SD = 2.9%). Interestingly, 
nonadherence prediction models outperformed churn prediction models in Vivira, as evidenced by 
consistently higher performance metrics across all weeks. This can be partly attributed to the greater 
class imbalance between adherent and nonadherent users compared to churned and retained users. 
However, the higher performance of nonadherence models even in the early weeks, when class 
imbalances were similar to those in churn prediction models, suggests that the methodologies are 
particularly well-suited for predicting nonadherence relative to the intervention’s intended use.  
In contrast, the performance of nonadherence prediction models in Manoa was comparatively 
lower, correctly identifying an average of 86% (SD = 7.6%, mean AUC = 0.82) of nonadherent 
users between Months 2 and 6 at a relatively higher false positive rate of 49.5% (SD = 12.9%).  
Feature importance analyses across all prediction models showed that behavioral app engagement 
data collected closer to the prediction event had a stronger impact on model performance. This 
finding aligns with previous research [5, 21, 29, 30] and explains the lower performance observed 
in Manoa, where nonadherence was measured monthly rather than weekly, limiting the availability 
of recent behavioral data near the prediction event. These results underscore the importance of using 
data in close temporal proximity to the prediction event for improving model performance, 
highlighting a critical consideration for the development of predictive models. 
Daily churn prediction models demonstrated nearly identical performance across the two 
independent mHealth interventions, highlighting the generalizability of our approach. These models 
correctly identified an average of 84.4% (SD = 19.1%, mean AUC = 0.87) of users between Days 
1 and 82 in Vivira, and 86% (SD = 14.3%, mean AUC = 0.87) of users between Days 1 and 178 in 

 22 
Manoa, who recorded their last login before the end of the 7-day prediction window. False positive 
rates were comparably lower, averaging 29.2% (SD = 8.5%) in Vivira and 25.8% (SD = 6.1%) in 
Manoa. 
Our results further show that the predictive performance of daily churn prediction models improves 
over time as more behavioral app engagement data becomes available. This finding aligns with 
prior research, which primarily focused on the early weeks of user engagement in mHealth 
interventions [4, 20]. Notably, as class imbalances declined between Day 1 and Day 25 in Vivira 
and Day 1 and Day 72 in Manoa, and then increased thereafter, model performance continued to 
improve. This trend underscores the robustness of these predictive models, which maintained high 
accuracy across these extended program durations from Day 4 forward. 
In summary, our study reinforces the applicability of past behavioral app engagement data for 
making daily churn predictions over extended durations. This applicability has been suggested in 
previous mHealth intervention studies [5, 21, 30] and across other app domains such as gaming, 
education, and social media [7, 27, 36, 45, 51, 62, 65]. However, these prior studies generally 
focused on predicting churn at specific points in time and shorter durations, whereas our study 
demonstrates its applicability for daily predictions over extended program durations. Furthermore, 
this study is the first to establish the applicability of these predictive methodologies for 
nonadherence relative to intended use, as defined by Sieverink et al. (2017). This distinction 
highlights the broader utility of such models in the context of mHealth interventions. 
4.2 The Potential for Targeted Strategies to Promote Adherence 
Following evaluations by Jakob et al. (2024), we assessed how many users record another log in 
after a correct nonadherence or churn prediction to shed light on the potential for targeted strategies 
promoting adherence before churn occurs. 
While nonadherence prediction models were more adept at identifying nonadherent users who had 
already churned, they also correctly identified a substantial proportion of nonadherent users before 
they recorded their last log in. In Vivira, weekly nonadherence prediction models correctly 
identified an average of 98.3% (SD = 1.6%) of nonadherent users who recorded their last login 
before the 7-day prediction window, 82.6% (SD = 7.1%) of nonadherent users who recorded their 
last login within the 7-day prediction window, and 83.4% (SD = 3.4%) of nonadherent users who 
recorded their last login after the prediction window. In Manoa, monthly nonadherence prediction 
models correctly identified an average of 97.1% (SD = 2.9%) of nonadherent users who recorded 
their last login before the 31-day prediction window, 92% (SD = 5.2%) of users recording their last 
login within the 31-day prediction window, and 74.9% (SD = 4.3%) of nonadherent users who 
recorded their last login after the 31-day prediction window. 

 
23 
Churn prediction models identified churned users (those who recorded their last login before the 7-
day prediction window) more accurately than churning users (those who recorded their last login 
within the 7-day prediction window). In Vivira, churn prediction models detected an average of 
88.1% (SD = 19.1%) of churned users and an average of 51.9% (SD = 14.7%) of churning across 
daily prediction models from Day 1 until Day 84. In Manoa, churn prediction models detected 
88.2% (SD = 12.9%) of churned users and 51.5% (SD = 18%) of churning users across daily 
predictions from Day 1 until Day 178. 
These findings highlight that nonadherence prediction models are not only effective in identifying 
users who have already discontinued app use but can also detect users in the early stages of 
disengagement. Since many of these users continue to log in after being flagged, such models 
present an opportunity to implement targeted preventive strategies directly within the app. These 
strategies could extend beyond win-back efforts delivered through external channels (e.g., emails, 
phone calls) and instead focus on proactive measures such as system adaptations (e.g., tailoring 
persuasive elements or adjusting behavioral goals), active in-app interventions (e.g., personalized 
push notifications), or the integration of complementary intervention components (e.g., monetary 
incentives or human support). Since some adherence-promoting strategies, such as monetary 
incentives or human support, incur utilization costs, selectively targeting users at the highest risk of 
nonadherence could also support the cost-effectiveness of mHealth interventions. 
4.3 Implications for Researchers and Providers 
The results of our study demonstrate that ML algorithms, when paired with behavioral app 
engagement data, can generate actionable insights that may support targeted strategies for 
preventing nonadherence. One promising aspect is that the app activity features used in this study 
- daily app activity and daily session counts - are not only predictive but generally applicable to any 
mHealth intervention that uses a mobile app as a primary intervention component. Likewise, the 
number of daily completed exercises used in Vivira corresponds directly to the app’s intended use. 
This concept can be extended to various interventions: an educational app may leverage the daily 
number of completed quizzes, while a physical activity program could track the number of physical 
activities logged, or a smoking cessation app might use the frequency of smoking diary entries as 
features for their predictive model. 
Previous research has consistently ranked features related to user app activity (e.g., daily logins) 
and app progress (e.g., completion of app-logged activities) as the most important for churn 
prediction in mHealth interventions [5, 21] and other app domains [7, 27, 29, 41, 56]. Our findings 
align with these observations, with such behavioral features demonstrating high predictive accuracy 
even over extended prediction periods. 

 24 
In contrast, prior research on adherence to mHealth interventions has often emphasized contextual 
factors over behavioral ones. Prior digital health studies typically focus on sociodemographic data 
such as age, gender, income, education, pre-existing health conditions, or specific intervention 
components as predictors of adherence [20]. While these analyses can provide valuable insights, 
our results suggest that simple app engagement features, such as daily app activity, are sufficient to 
predict future user behavior. This finding is also consistent with previous churn prediction studies 
in DHIs, where adding contextual features to models already incorporating behavioral app 
engagement features did not improve predictive performance [5, 21]. 
Consequently, researchers and providers of mHealth interventions are encouraged to utilize 
behavioral app engagement features when constructing nonadherence prediction models. This 
approach offers a novel perspective on nonadherence prediction, which may be uniquely enabled 
by digital interventions due to their capacity to collect objective and granular user behavior data, 
which is typically not available in non-digital interventions. 
Multiple ways exist to further optimize the presented prediction models. Prior research has shown 
that different ML algorithms can yield varying outcomes, with some performing better across 
different app contexts. Examples of algorithms frequently reported as best-performing for churn 
prediction across various app domains are Logistic Regression [5, 66], Random Forest [14, 21, 39, 
45, 59], Boosting models (e.g., XGBoost) [15, 35, 56, 57], and Recurrent Neural Networks (e.g., 
LSTMs) [22, 27, 29, 65]. Hence, researchers and developers are advised to evaluate multiple 
algorithms to identify the most suitable ML algorithms for their specific classification problem, 
also considering their complexity, which influences development time, resource consumption, and 
model explainability. 
Feature sets can also be expanded to include more intervention-specific attributes, such as social 
features (e.g., number of interactions between users) in DHIs with social networking components 
or transactional features (e.g., number of in-app purchases) in DHIs with payment options, which 
have been shown to enhance predictive performance in other app domains [30, 32, 39, 42, 56]. 
Including additional features may be particularly beneficial during the early stages when user 
activity features may not yet provide a strong predictive signal, as highlighted by the insufficient 
performance of our churn prediction models in the first three days. 
In summary, our findings underscore the potential of generalizable, behavioral app engagement 
data for the prediction of nonadherence in mHealth interventions. These features, combined with 
accessible ML algorithms, offer a practical foundation for researchers and providers of mHealth 
interventions planning to develop and implement predictive models for nonadherence. 

 
25 
4.4 Limitations and Future Work 
This study used historical app engagement data to predict nonadherence. While the presented results 
are promising, prospective trials are necessary to fully establish the applicability of these models. 
Nevertheless, our findings align with prior research on churn prediction in DHIs [5, 21]. Notably, 
the strong performance of our models across two distinct mHealth interventions suggests that the 
approach – utilizing behavioral app engagement features in combination with ML algorithms – has 
the potential to be widely applicable across various mHealth intervention contexts to predict 
nonadherence. 
One potential limitation of the Vivira dataset is the exclusion of users who did not provide the 
required consent to use their engagement data for research purposes, thereby limiting the analysis 
to users who agreed to participate. If non-consenting users exhibit different behaviors, the model’s 
performance may not fully represent the broader population. However, since the same 
methodologies achieved comparable results in the Manoa dataset – distinct in its regulatory 
environment, addressed medical condition, program duration, user demographics, and therapeutic 
approach - the applied methods are likely generalizable across different mHealth contexts and 
populations. 
A shared characteristic of both analyzed mHealth interventions is that users must provide proof of 
medical need to access the apps and receive reimbursement. User behavior in these contexts may 
differ from that observed in mHealth interventions directly available in public app stores, where 
users can self-enroll. The two mHealth interventions, however, also differ in their onboarding 
channels – the DiGA Vivira is either directly prescribed by a physician, or access is requested by a 
patient with a confirmed diagnosis, while Manoa is actively promoted by health insurance providers 
–  supporting the generalizability of our findings across varied onboarding contexts. However, it is 
noteworthy that the onboarding context, users’ trust in the DHI provider, and users’ health 
conditions may impact adherence [20]. Hence, another important aspect of the mHealth 
interventions analyzed is their relatively high user retention rates. A study by Baumel et al. (2019) 
compared average retention rates for mental health apps at approximately 10% on Day 7 and 3.3% 
on Day 30 across 59 analyzed apps [2]. In contrast, the two mHealth interventions examined in this 
study demonstrated substantially higher retention rates: 32% and 53% on Day 7, and 19% and 27% 
on Day 30, respectively. DHIs with substantially lower retention rates may face challenges in 
applying the methods described here, due to class imbalance between engaged and disengaged 
users. This imbalance can complicate the training and evaluation of prediction models, highlighting 
the need for further research in contexts where disengagement is more prevalent. 
The nonadherence prediction models described in this study also rely on the availability of rich, 
continuous behavioral app engagement data. This dependency suggests that these models are most 
effective in systems designed for frequent, ongoing use, where user engagement data is naturally 

 26 
generated over time. In settings where engagement data is sparse, the performance of prediction 
models may be diminished. Similarly, a 7-day prediction window, while ideal for timely 
intervention, may not be suitable for mHealth interventions that are not intended for regular weekly 
use. Different methods and prediction windows may be required to capture user churn accurately 
for interventions with more sporadic or irregular usage patterns. 
An additional consideration is that our analyses were tied to a predefined observation window 
related to a full program duration of the apps. Although predictions were made from Day 1 through 
Day 84 and Day 1 through Day 178, using a 7-day prediction window to account for the entire 
period up to Days 90 and 186, respectively, a user who last logs in during the final week of the 
cycle may not be a "churned" user but rather a user who stops using the app because their program 
duration ends. Conversely, users who have not logged in for a month before the end of the 
observation window can also start another program, indicating that churn status can be ambiguous 
at the end of fixed observation periods. 
While our results suggest that prediction models can accurately predict who is likely to become 
nonadherent and when, they do not provide insights into the underlying reasons why users 
disengage. Nevertheless, they could serve as valuable research tools, detecting early signs of 
nonadherence and prompting targeted questionnaires to understand disengagement reasons before 
a user is lost to follow-up. This approach could particularly help identifying factors driving 
nonadherence in real-world contexts, where once a user fully disengages, it becomes difficult to 
gather such information [47]. 
It is also important to recognize that adherence to mHealth interventions is an intermediate outcome. 
The primary aim of mHealth interventions is to facilitate health behavior change and ultimately 
improve health outcomes. Although studies suggest a positive association between adherence and 
health outcomes, the link between adherence to mHealth interventions and health outcomes is not 
fully understood and needs further investigation in diverse settings [6]. While evidence from other 
app domains suggests that combining churn prediction models with preventive strategies – such as 
personalized push notifications, omnichannel nudges, or content adaptations – can reduce churn 
[14, 33, 35], it also remains unclear whether this targeted approach can improve adherence and, 
ultimately, health outcomes. Given the relatively new application of churn prediction models in 
mHealth interventions and this study being the first to comprehensively evaluate nonadherence 
prediction models aligned with the definition by Sieverink et al. (2017), significant research gaps 
remain.  
Future research should aim to replicate nonadherence prediction models in diverse mHealth 
contexts and evaluate their integration with targeted preventive strategies in prospective trials to 
assess the impact of these combined approaches on app usage, adherence, and health outcomes. 

 
27 
Addressing these gaps will support the development of more adaptive and impactful mHealth 
interventions and their potential to mitigate the rising prevalence and economic burden of NCDs.

1 
Predicting Nonadherence to Mobile Health Interventions 
Planned Publication: Jakob R, Benning L, Sévin CM, Von Wangenheim F, Fleisch E, Kowatsch 
T. Predicting Nonadherence to Mobile Health Interventions. In: (2025) (In preparation)

Abstract 
The rising prevalence and economic burden of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) present a 
significant challenge to patients and healthcare systems, calling for innovative, scalable, and cost-
effective solutions. Mobile health (mHealth) interventions, facilitated by the ubiquity of 
smartphones, have emerged as promising tools to support the prevention and management of NCDs. 
Yet, despite growing evidence and availability, mHealth interventions face high nonadherence, 
where users fail to use these tools as intended or discontinue use entirely before achieving desired 
outcomes. The rich data collected by mHealth interventions raise the question of whether – and to 
what extent – nonadherence can be predicted using these data. If so, such predictions could inform 
targeted strategies aimed at preventing nonadherence before it fully manifests. We developed 
machine learning models for the prediction of nonadherence in two mHealth interventions, one for 
nonspecific and degenerative back pain over a program duration of 90 days (Vivira, n = 8,372), and 
another for hypertension self-management over 186 days (Manoa, n = 6,674). Our models identified 
an average of 94% of nonadherent users between Weeks 2 and 13 in Vivira (mean AUC = 0.95), 
defined as completing fewer than eight therapeutic exercises per week. In Manoa, our models 
correctly identified an average of 86% of nonadherent users between months 2 and 6 (mean AUC 
= 0.82), defined as completing fewer than one blood pressure measurement week per month. 
Additionally, models predicting churn (users’ last login within program duration) achieved mean 
AUCs of 0.87 for both apps, correctly identifying 84-86% of churned users. These findings 
demonstrate that nonadherence can be accurately predicted, highlighting a unique and underutilized 
advantage of mHealth interventions – the ability to transform app engagement data into actionable 
insights that may inform targeted strategies to promote adherence.

2 
1 Introduction 
Digital health interventions (DHIs) have demonstrated the potential to assist patients and healthcare 
systems in addressing the global rise and financial impact of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), 
which are the leading causes of death and disability worldwide [16, 26, 44, 64]. In particular, mobile 
health (mHealth) interventions have emerged as versatile tools to promote behavior change among 
patients, improve health outcomes, and reduce healthcare costs due to the widespread availability 
of smartphones [8, 38, 49, 60]. A growing body of evidence suggests that mHealth interventions 
can effectively support the prevention and management of NCDs by addressing modifiable risk 
factors, including physical inactivity [52, 53], unhealthy diets [67], tobacco use [63], the harmful 
use of alcohol [12] and metabolic risk factors such as obesity [52], hypertension [1], and 
hyperglycemia [19]. Furthermore, mHealth interventions show promise in improving mental health 
conditions, including depression and anxiety [10, 31]. In light of this, first healthcare systems with 
population-wide coverage now include mHealth interventions as reimbursable items in patient 
coverage, and prescriptions for mHealth interventions are starting to become a more common part 
of treatment plans and health insurance benefits packages [13, 25, 48, 58]. In Germany, for example, 
mHealth interventions have been introduced as prescription digital therapies (PDT) to the 
collectively funded statutory health insurance (SHI) system with scalable reimbursement strategies 
under the German Digital Healthcare Act in 2019 [46]. While the SHI system provides coverage 
for approximately 90% of the German population, a private health insurance (PHI) system covers 
the remaining proportion of the coverage to meet the legal requirement of universal health insurance 
coverage of the German population [4]. Similar to the SHI system, the PHI system is exploring 
options of digital care and is expanding its spectrum of PDT solutions. 
However, despite the increasing availability and demonstrated efficacy of mHealth interventions, a 
substantial proportion of users fail to adhere to these programs as intended or disengage 
prematurely, posing a major barrier to their effectiveness [9, 18]. Although the specific metrics used 
to quantify adherence vary across DHI studies, there is broad consensus that adherence is 
suboptimal. A systematic review focusing on mHealth interventions for chronic diseases (17 
studies) reported a pooled dropout rate of 43%, with observational studies exhibiting a higher rate 
(49%) compared to more controlled randomized controlled trials (40%) [34]. Another review of 83 
web-based interventions concluded that only half of users adhered to the interventions [24]. A study 
evaluating user engagement with 59 mental health apps found that fewer than 10% of users logged 
in daily after seven days, and by Day 15, the median open rate had declined to 3.9% [2]. Additional 
research corroborates these findings, with up to 80% of users of mHealth interventions engaging 
only at a minimal level, logging into mHealth apps no more than once, and failing to use the apps 
consistently over extended periods [11, 34, 43].

3 
The growing body of literature on mHealth interventions also highlights the need for more rigorous 
approaches to measuring adherence to DHIs. Sieverink et al. (2017) noted that adherence remains 
an underdeveloped and often improperly utilized concept in the existing literature [50]. Their 
review of 62 studies revealed that 34 studies operationalized adherence as “the more use, the better,” 
while only 28 studies established a clear threshold for the intended use of the technology. To 
enhance the comparability and reliability of adherence measurements, they proposed that future 
studies should define adherence based on a specific threshold aligned with the technology’s 
intended use, also ensuring that this intended use is clearly defined and justified [50]. This definition 
distinguishes nonadherence from the concept of churn – also referred to as dropout, abandonment, 
or attrition – which is considered a key indicator for the adoption and success of mobile applications 
[17, 35]. Churn refers to a user discontinuing use of a mobile application entirely and is thus closely 
related to nonadherence and can be viewed as a severe form of nonadherence. 
While the prediction of nonadherence in accordance with the definition of Sieverink et al. (2017) 
constitutes a research gap, a growing body of research suggests that churn in mHealth interventions 
can be accurately predicted based on behavioral app engagement data (e.g., app login or session 
counts) [5, 14, 30, 37, 40, 57]. However, existing studies have predicted churn only at specific 
points in time, leaving limited evidence on prediction performances at different stages of the user 
journey. Likewise, it is unclear to what extent prediction models can predict churn before users 
fully disengage. Addressing this research gap, Jakob et al. (2024) recently predicted churn at the 
end of each day of users’ initial week of usage in a public digital weight loss intervention, also 
testing a wide range of features and ML algorithms. The best-performing model in this study was a 
random forest model that only used daily login counts, achieving an F1 score of 0.87 (AUC = 0.73, 
Accuracy = 81%) on Day 7 and an average F1 score of 0.84 over the initial week (mean AUC = 
0.71, mean Accuracy = 0.76). Churn prediction models in this study improved in terms of F1, AUC, 
and Accuracy from Day 1 to Day 7, hinting at a progressive improvement in churn prediction over 
time. Notably, the study also analyzed the number of users who reengaged with the app after a 
correct churn prediction to assess the potential of in-app interventions to prevent churn. The best-
performing model correctly predicted an average of 93% of churned users over the initial week with 
a mean false positive rate of 58.7%, and correctly predicted 81% of churned users who would 
reengage after a correct churn prediction. These findings suggest that prediction models may not 
only serve as early detection tools but can provide actionable insights for the delivery of targeted 
strategies to promote adherence before users fully disengage. However, the study also noted a 
shortcoming regarding a restricted focus on the initial week of app usage, calling for further studies 
in diverse settings with extended observation windows to assess how the predictive performance 
and the potential for mitigation strategies evolve over extended periods [21].

4 
This study addresses this research gap by evaluating nonadherence prediction models in two distinct 
mHealth interventions (Vivira and Manoa) across different regulatory environments (i.e. SHI and 
PHI), medical conditions addressed (i.e. nonspecific back pain and arterial hypertension), program 
durations (i.e. 90 and 186 days), user demographics, as well as different therapeutic approaches (i.e. 
guided movement therapy and personalized hypertension self-management). To provide a 
comprehensive perspective, we predict nonadherence relative to the intended use of the 
interventions, following the definition by Sieverink et al. (2017), as well as its most severe form: 
churn (i.e., complete discontinuation). Building on Jakob et al. (2024), we also examine the 
proportion of users who reengage after a correct prediction, offering insights into the potential for 
targeted strategies to promote adherence before churn occurs. Through these analyses, we aim to 
determine the extent to which nonadherence to mHealth interventions can be predicted. 
2 Methods 
2.1 Datasets and Definitions of Nonadherence 
2.1.1 Vivira 
The first anonymized dataset was collected from “Vivira”, a CE-marked Medical Device 
Regulation risk class I mHealth intervention for nonspecific and degenerative backpain which is 
approved as a “Digitale Gesundheitsanwendung” (DiGA) in the regulatory environment for PDTs 
in the German SHI system [46]. As a DiGA, the medical effectiveness of Vivira was confirmed by 
the German Federal Institute for Medicines and Medical Devices (Bundesinstitut für Arzneimittel 
und Medizinprodukte, BfArM) , a regulatory body, based on a confirmatory study [61]. Further 
research supports the real-world effectiveness of Vivira [54, 55]. Under DiGA regulations, Vivira 
is available to all patients covered by the SHI system, but only accessible upon prescription by a 
qualified healthcare professional or upon a patient providing proof of medical need to their 
respective health insurance. A DiGA prescription for Vivira allows full access to the respective 
DiGA for 90 days. The Vivira app provides individualized and guided exercises for asynchronous 
and decentralized movement therapy. Educational content (e.g., exercise introductions, annotated 
video cues, information on the medical condition, and therapy principles) and behavioral cues (e.g., 
visualizations of therapy progress, reminders) prompt patients to interact with the app and support 
retention. The program aims to improve pain, mobility, strength, and coordination. Vivira is 
available for iOS and Android devices. 
The use of DiGA data is strictly limited. Therefore, only users who provided consent under Article 
4, Section 2, 4 of the DiGA regulations (DiGA-Verordnung, DiGAV) were included. The dataset 
included data from 8,372 users who activated their first prescription between January 1, 2023, and 
March 31, 2024. Of the included users who provided information on their gender (98%, 
8,208/8,372), 68.3% were female, 31.6% were male, and 0.1% non-binary. Among users who

5 
provided information on their age range (99%, 8,251/8,372), 25% were aged 18–35 years, 23% 
were 36–45 years, 24% were 46–55 years, 21.1% were 56–65 years, 6.4% were 66–75 years, and 
1% were over 75 years old. 
For each user, binary daily activity data (active or inactive) was available based on whether the user 
triggered any app event on any day during their first 90-day prescription period. The dataset also 
included the number of exercises completed by each user on each day during the 90-day prescription 
period.  
The intended use of Vivira involves completing weekly exercises. The instruction for use 
recommends at least three sessions per week, each consisting of four independent exercises with 
accompanying audiovisual instructions and guidance. Yet, using a propensity score matching 
approach, Klingenberg et al. (2023) illustrated that a significantly higher probability of achieving a 
clinically meaningful improvement of pain intensity by the time of churn is already achieved by 
users who complete at least two sessions per week [28]. We therefore deem a minimum exercise 
frequency of two sessions (i.e. eight exercises) per week the minimum adherence to yield clinically 
relevant therapeutic benefits from the use of Vivira. Therefore, adherence was measured weekly, 
defined as completing eight or more exercises per week. Users with fewer than eight exercises per 
week were considered nonadherent. 
2.1.2 Manoa 
The second anonymized dataset was collected from "Manoa," a mHealth intervention designed for 
hypertension self-management. The Manoa app features a conversational agent (CA; a chatbot 
simulating conversation with human users) that collects user data and provides guidance on various 
health aspects, including lifestyle choices and medication adherence. Manoa is accessible to 
customers of seven of the ten largest private health insurance companies in the German and two of 
the ten largest in the Swiss PHI system. Manoa is available to individuals diagnosed with 
hypertension. Participating health insurance companies provide interested users with access codes 
for full six-month access. The app's core feature is a blood pressure diary. The CA offers 
personalized feedback on blood pressure levels based on a structured home blood pressure 
monitoring protocol, which has been associated with a reduction in average blood pressure and 
improvement in blood pressure control [3]. The app recommends scheduling a doctor's appointment 
if blood pressure levels are elevated. Users can share their blood pressure report digitally with their 
doctor or export it as a PDF. Manoa promotes regular monitoring through reminders, tracking, and 
motivational messages from the CA. Blood pressure data can be entered manually, scanned using 
the smartphone's camera, or imported directly from compatible measurement devices. Users are 
prompted to measure their blood pressure twice daily for six days during each home blood pressure 
monitoring period. Manoa is available for iOS and Android devices.

6 
The dataset included data from a total of 6,674 users. Of the included users who provided 
information on their gender (82.8%; 5,523/6,674), 21.7% were female and 78.3% were male. 
Among users who provided information on their age range (83.1%; 5,548/6,674), 0.9% were aged 
18–29 years, 6.1% were 30–44 years, 16.8% were 45–54 years, 34% were 55–64 years, 32.8% were 
65–74 years, and 9.4% were 75 years or older. 
For each user, the number of daily app sessions (continuous) during the 186-day program duration 
was available from which binary daily activity data (active or inactive) could be derived. 
The intended use of Manoa aligns with medical guidelines from the European Society of 
Hypertension (ESH) and European Society of Cardiology (ESC), recommending blood pressure 
measurements for 3-6 days once a month. After the initial period in the first month, the app sends 
periodic reminders every four weeks to continue monitoring with users being able adjust the timing 
of their home blood pressure monitoring periods. Adherence was measured monthly from months 
2 to 6 after the initial period, defined as completing at least one measurement week per month 
consisting of at least 3 within 7 days with morning and evening measurements. Users who did not 
complete a measurement week per month were considered nonadherent. 
2.2 Feature Selection, Model Training, and Evaluation 
Aligning with previous churn prediction studies that achieved accurate prediction results with daily 
behavioral app engagement features in the initial week of usage in DHIs for weight loss and 
smoking cessation [5, 21], we selected generalizable daily app engagement features related to users' 
activity and progress with the DHIs in this study. This choice is also consistent with churn 
prediction studies in other app domains, which have ranked features related to user app activity 
(e.g., daily logins) and app progress (e.g., completion of app-logged activities) as the most 
important features [7, 27, 29, 41, 56]. 
In Vivira, we predicted nonadherence weekly from Weeks 2 to 13 based on users’ daily app activity 
variables (active or inactive) and the daily number of completed exercises variables (continuous) 
of the preceding weeks. To illustrate this with an example, for the prediction of nonadherence in 
Week 2 (a user completing fewer than 8 exercises between Days 8 to 14), we utilized users’ daily 
app activity variables from Days 1 until 7 and the daily number of completed exercises from Days 
1 until 7. 
In Manoa, we predicted nonadherence monthly from Months 2 to 6 based on users’ daily app 
activity variables (active or inactive) and the number of daily app sessions (continuous) of the 
preceding months. To illustrate this with an example, for the prediction of nonadherence in Month 
2 (a user completing no measurement week between Days 32 to 63), we utilized users’ daily app 
activity variables from Days 1 until 31 and the number of daily app sessions from Days 1 until 31.

7 
Additionally, we predicted churn (users’ last login within program duration) daily in Vivira (at the 
end of Days 1 to 82) and Manoa (at the end of Days 1 until 178) with a 7-Day prediction window 
based on features from previous days. To illustrate this with an example, for the prediction of churn 
at the end of Day 14, we predicted if the users’ last login occurs until the end of Day 21 based on 
input features from Days 1 until 14. The choice of a 7-day prediction window was based on the 
DHIs’ intended weekly use and seven days of inactivity, which are commonly used to define churn 
in other churn prediction studies [7, 23, 33, 36, 57, 62, 65]. 
Consistent with the aforementioned study by Jakob et al. (2024), we applied random forest 
algorithms for all predictions [21]. This choice is further supported by prediction studies in other 
app domains that achieved superior performance with random forest models across multiple tested 
ML algorithms [14, 21, 39, 45, 59]. We preprocessed available features by normalizing numerical 
data by performing square root scaling for right-skewed data and standard scaling for non-right-
skewed data. For nonadherence prediction in Vivira and churn prediction in both mHealth 
interventions, we randomly split 80% of the dataset into a training set (Vivira = 6,697, Manoa = 
5,339) and the remaining 20% into a test set (Vivira = 1,675, Manoa = 1,335). For nonadherence 
prediction in Manoa, we only included users who completed the initial blood pressure measurement 
week (n = 2,095), resulting in 1,676 users in the training set and 419 users in the test set. 
We applied stratified 10-fold cross-validation and randomized search for hyperparameter tuning 
on the training sets, optimizing for F1 score for all models. Additionally, we applied Tomek Links 
undersampling to the training data to address class imbalance class before cross-validation [15]. 
Detailed hyperparameter grids are provided in Appendix 6.1. 
We evaluated model performance using F1 score, area under the curve (AUC), accuracy, precision, 
and recall. We also conducted feature importance analyses for each model to compare which 
features contribute the most to their predictive performance. 
To assess the intervention potential, we further categorized and distinguished between “churned 
users” (last login before prediction window), “churning users” (last login within prediction 
window), and “active users” (last login after prediction window). To illustrate this with an example, 
for a prediction at the end of Day 7 for the prediction window between Days 8 and 14, a user with 
a last login on Day 6 is considered “churned”, a user with a last login on Day 12 is considered

3.1 Descriptive Results 
3.1.1 Vivira 
Vivira users were active on an average of 15.5 days (SD = 19.6) and completed an average of 55.6 
exercises (SD = 76.5) during the 90-day program duration. The mean last day of logging into the 
app across all users was 38.5 (SD = 31.7). On a weekly basis, users were active for an average of 
4.9 weeks (SD = 4.0) and adherent for an average of 3.1 weeks (SD = 3.9) throughout the 
observation period. The mean number of weekly active days decreased from 3.1 (SD = 2.0) in Week 
1 to 0.4 (SD = 1.2) in Week 13, while the mean number of completed exercises decreased from 9.7 
(SD = 9.2) in Week 1 to 1.4 (SD = 4.4) in Week 13, indicating a progressive decrease in user 
engagement over time. Detailed descriptive statistics are provided in Appendix Tables 6.5 to 6.7. 
As highlighted in Figure 6.1, user churn was most severe at the beginning of the program with 
approximately 25% of users recording their last login during the first week and 8.8% in the second 
week. From Week 3 through Week 12, the relative churn rate remained relatively stable, within 
4.2% to 6.5% of users logging their last activity in each respective week until Week 13, in which 
13.2% of users remained active and thus recorded their last login in the final week.
