4 Discussion 
4.1 Predicting Nonadherence to Mobile Health Interventions 
Our findings show that nonadherence to mHealth interventions can be accurately predicted over 
extended program durations, both in terms of adherence relative to intended use as defined by 
Sieverink et al. (2017) and in its most severe form – churn (i.e., complete discontinuation of use). 
Our study thus extends prior research showing that methodologies effective in predicting churn 
during the first week [21], remain applicable over longer durations of 90 and 186 days across two 
distinct mHealth interventions to predict nonadherence. Given the conceptual link between churn 
and nonadherence – where fully disengaged users are inherently nonadherent – these results are 
intuitive. Our descriptive analysis further emphasizes this relationship, showing that the decline in 
adherence over time in Vivira and Manoa is largely driven by churn (i.e. users discontinuing 
entirely). 
Weekly nonadherence prediction models in Vivira achieved strong performance, correctly 
identifying an average of 94.2% (SD = 4.2%, mean AUC = 0.95) of nonadherent users between 
Weeks 2 and 13, with an average false positive rate of 24.2% (SD = 2.9%). Interestingly, 
nonadherence prediction models outperformed churn prediction models in Vivira, as evidenced by 
consistently higher performance metrics across all weeks. This can be partly attributed to the greater 
class imbalance between adherent and nonadherent users compared to churned and retained users. 
However, the higher performance of nonadherence models even in the early weeks, when class 
imbalances were similar to those in churn prediction models, suggests that the methodologies are 
particularly well-suited for predicting nonadherence relative to the intervention’s intended use.  
In contrast, the performance of nonadherence prediction models in Manoa was comparatively 
lower, correctly identifying an average of 86% (SD = 7.6%, mean AUC = 0.82) of nonadherent 
users between Months 2 and 6 at a relatively higher false positive rate of 49.5% (SD = 12.9%).  
Feature importance analyses across all prediction models showed that behavioral app engagement 
data collected closer to the prediction event had a stronger impact on model performance. This 
finding aligns with previous research [5, 21, 29, 30] and explains the lower performance observed 
in Manoa, where nonadherence was measured monthly rather than weekly, limiting the availability 
of recent behavioral data near the prediction event. These results underscore the importance of using 
data in close temporal proximity to the prediction event for improving model performance, 
highlighting a critical consideration for the development of predictive models. 
Daily churn prediction models demonstrated nearly identical performance across the two 
independent mHealth interventions, highlighting the generalizability of our approach. These models 
correctly identified an average of 84.4% (SD = 19.1%, mean AUC = 0.87) of users between Days 
1 and 82 in Vivira, and 86% (SD = 14.3%, mean AUC = 0.87) of users between Days 1 and 178 in

22 
Manoa, who recorded their last login before the end of the 7-day prediction window. False positive 
rates were comparably lower, averaging 29.2% (SD = 8.5%) in Vivira and 25.8% (SD = 6.1%) in 
Manoa. 
Our results further show that the predictive performance of daily churn prediction models improves 
over time as more behavioral app engagement data becomes available. This finding aligns with 
prior research, which primarily focused on the early weeks of user engagement in mHealth 
interventions [4, 20]. Notably, as class imbalances declined between Day 1 and Day 25 in Vivira 
and Day 1 and Day 72 in Manoa, and then increased thereafter, model performance continued to 
improve. This trend underscores the robustness of these predictive models, which maintained high 
accuracy across these extended program durations from Day 4 forward. 
In summary, our study reinforces the applicability of past behavioral app engagement data for 
making daily churn predictions over extended durations. This applicability has been suggested in 
previous mHealth intervention studies [5, 21, 30] and across other app domains such as gaming, 
education, and social media [7, 27, 36, 45, 51, 62, 65]. However, these prior studies generally 
focused on predicting churn at specific points in time and shorter durations, whereas our study 
demonstrates its applicability for daily predictions over extended program durations. Furthermore, 
this study is the first to establish the applicability of these predictive methodologies for 
nonadherence relative to intended use, as defined by Sieverink et al. (2017). This distinction 
highlights the broader utility of such models in the context of mHealth interventions. 
4.2 The Potential for Targeted Strategies to Promote Adherence 
Following evaluations by Jakob et al. (2024), we assessed how many users record another log in 
after a correct nonadherence or churn prediction to shed light on the potential for targeted strategies 
promoting adherence before churn occurs. 
While nonadherence prediction models were more adept at identifying nonadherent users who had 
already churned, they also correctly identified a substantial proportion of nonadherent users before 
they recorded their last log in. In Vivira, weekly nonadherence prediction models correctly 
identified an average of 98.3% (SD = 1.6%) of nonadherent users who recorded their last login 
before the 7-day prediction window, 82.6% (SD = 7.1%) of nonadherent users who recorded their 
last login within the 7-day prediction window, and 83.4% (SD = 3.4%) of nonadherent users who 
recorded their last login after the prediction window. In Manoa, monthly nonadherence prediction 
models correctly identified an average of 97.1% (SD = 2.9%) of nonadherent users who recorded 
their last login before the 31-day prediction window, 92% (SD = 5.2%) of users recording their last 
login within the 31-day prediction window, and 74.9% (SD = 4.3%) of nonadherent users who 
recorded their last login after the 31-day prediction window.

23 
Churn prediction models identified churned users (those who recorded their last login before the 7-
day prediction window) more accurately than churning users (those who recorded their last login 
within the 7-day prediction window). In Vivira, churn prediction models detected an average of 
88.1% (SD = 19.1%) of churned users and an average of 51.9% (SD = 14.7%) of churning across 
daily prediction models from Day 1 until Day 84. In Manoa, churn prediction models detected 
88.2% (SD = 12.9%) of churned users and 51.5% (SD = 18%) of churning users across daily 
predictions from Day 1 until Day 178. 
These findings highlight that nonadherence prediction models are not only effective in identifying 
users who have already discontinued app use but can also detect users in the early stages of 
disengagement. Since many of these users continue to log in after being flagged, such models 
present an opportunity to implement targeted preventive strategies directly within the app. These 
strategies could extend beyond win-back efforts delivered through external channels (e.g., emails, 
phone calls) and instead focus on proactive measures such as system adaptations (e.g., tailoring 
persuasive elements or adjusting behavioral goals), active in-app interventions (e.g., personalized 
push notifications), or the integration of complementary intervention components (e.g., monetary 
incentives or human support). Since some adherence-promoting strategies, such as monetary 
incentives or human support, incur utilization costs, selectively targeting users at the highest risk of 
nonadherence could also support the cost-effectiveness of mHealth interventions. 
4.3 Implications for Researchers and Providers 
The results of our study demonstrate that ML algorithms, when paired with behavioral app 
engagement data, can generate actionable insights that may support targeted strategies for 
preventing nonadherence. One promising aspect is that the app activity features used in this study 
- daily app activity and daily session counts - are not only predictive but generally applicable to any 
mHealth intervention that uses a mobile app as a primary intervention component. Likewise, the 
number of daily completed exercises used in Vivira corresponds directly to the app’s intended use. 
This concept can be extended to various interventions: an educational app may leverage the daily 
number of completed quizzes, while a physical activity program could track the number of physical 
activities logged, or a smoking cessation app might use the frequency of smoking diary entries as 
features for their predictive model. 
Previous research has consistently ranked features related to user app activity (e.g., daily logins) 
and app progress (e.g., completion of app-logged activities) as the most important for churn 
prediction in mHealth interventions [5, 21] and other app domains [7, 27, 29, 41, 56]. Our findings 
align with these observations, with such behavioral features demonstrating high predictive accuracy 
even over extended prediction periods.

24 
In contrast, prior research on adherence to mHealth interventions has often emphasized contextual 
factors over behavioral ones. Prior digital health studies typically focus on sociodemographic data 
such as age, gender, income, education, pre-existing health conditions, or specific intervention 
components as predictors of adherence [20]. While these analyses can provide valuable insights, 
our results suggest that simple app engagement features, such as daily app activity, are sufficient to 
predict future user behavior. This finding is also consistent with previous churn prediction studies 
in DHIs, where adding contextual features to models already incorporating behavioral app 
engagement features did not improve predictive performance [5, 21]. 
Consequently, researchers and providers of mHealth interventions are encouraged to utilize 
behavioral app engagement features when constructing nonadherence prediction models. This 
approach offers a novel perspective on nonadherence prediction, which may be uniquely enabled 
by digital interventions due to their capacity to collect objective and granular user behavior data, 
which is typically not available in non-digital interventions. 
Multiple ways exist to further optimize the presented prediction models. Prior research has shown 
that different ML algorithms can yield varying outcomes, with some performing better across 
different app contexts. Examples of algorithms frequently reported as best-performing for churn 
prediction across various app domains are Logistic Regression [5, 66], Random Forest [14, 21, 39, 
45, 59], Boosting models (e.g., XGBoost) [15, 35, 56, 57], and Recurrent Neural Networks (e.g., 
LSTMs) [22, 27, 29, 65]. Hence, researchers and developers are advised to evaluate multiple 
algorithms to identify the most suitable ML algorithms for their specific classification problem, 
also considering their complexity, which influences development time, resource consumption, and 
model explainability. 
Feature sets can also be expanded to include more intervention-specific attributes, such as social 
features (e.g., number of interactions between users) in DHIs with social networking components 
or transactional features (e.g., number of in-app purchases) in DHIs with payment options, which 
have been shown to enhance predictive performance in other app domains [30, 32, 39, 42, 56]. 
Including additional features may be particularly beneficial during the early stages when user 
activity features may not yet provide a strong predictive signal, as highlighted by the insufficient 
performance of our churn prediction models in the first three days. 
In summary, our findings underscore the potential of generalizable, behavioral app engagement 
data for the prediction of nonadherence in mHealth interventions. These features, combined with 
accessible ML algorithms, offer a practical foundation for researchers and providers of mHealth 
interventions planning to develop and implement predictive models for nonadherence.

25 
4.4 Limitations and Future Work 
This study used historical app engagement data to predict nonadherence. While the presented results 
are promising, prospective trials are necessary to fully establish the applicability of these models. 
Nevertheless, our findings align with prior research on churn prediction in DHIs [5, 21]. Notably, 
the strong performance of our models across two distinct mHealth interventions suggests that the 
approach – utilizing behavioral app engagement features in combination with ML algorithms – has 
the potential to be widely applicable across various mHealth intervention contexts to predict 
nonadherence. 
One potential limitation of the Vivira dataset is the exclusion of users who did not provide the 
required consent to use their engagement data for research purposes, thereby limiting the analysis 
to users who agreed to participate. If non-consenting users exhibit different behaviors, the model’s 
performance may not fully represent the broader population. However, since the same 
methodologies achieved comparable results in the Manoa dataset – distinct in its regulatory 
environment, addressed medical condition, program duration, user demographics, and therapeutic 
approach - the applied methods are likely generalizable across different mHealth contexts and 
populations. 
A shared characteristic of both analyzed mHealth interventions is that users must provide proof of 
medical need to access the apps and receive reimbursement. User behavior in these contexts may 
differ from that observed in mHealth interventions directly available in public app stores, where 
users can self-enroll. The two mHealth interventions, however, also differ in their onboarding 
channels – the DiGA Vivira is either directly prescribed by a physician, or access is requested by a 
patient with a confirmed diagnosis, while Manoa is actively promoted by health insurance providers 
–  supporting the generalizability of our findings across varied onboarding contexts. However, it is 
noteworthy that the onboarding context, users’ trust in the DHI provider, and users’ health 
conditions may impact adherence [20]. Hence, another important aspect of the mHealth 
interventions analyzed is their relatively high user retention rates. A study by Baumel et al. (2019) 
compared average retention rates for mental health apps at approximately 10% on Day 7 and 3.3% 
on Day 30 across 59 analyzed apps [2]. In contrast, the two mHealth interventions examined in this 
study demonstrated substantially higher retention rates: 32% and 53% on Day 7, and 19% and 27% 
on Day 30, respectively. DHIs with substantially lower retention rates may face challenges in 
applying the methods described here, due to class imbalance between engaged and disengaged 
users. This imbalance can complicate the training and evaluation of prediction models, highlighting 
the need for further research in contexts where disengagement is more prevalent. 
The nonadherence prediction models described in this study also rely on the availability of rich, 
continuous behavioral app engagement data. This dependency suggests that these models are most 
effective in systems designed for frequent, ongoing use, where user engagement data is naturally

26 
generated over time. In settings where engagement data is sparse, the performance of prediction 
models may be diminished. Similarly, a 7-day prediction window, while ideal for timely 
intervention, may not be suitable for mHealth interventions that are not intended for regular weekly 
use. Different methods and prediction windows may be required to capture user churn accurately 
for interventions with more sporadic or irregular usage patterns. 
An additional consideration is that our analyses were tied to a predefined observation window 
related to a full program duration of the apps. Although predictions were made from Day 1 through 
Day 84 and Day 1 through Day 178, using a 7-day prediction window to account for the entire 
period up to Days 90 and 186, respectively, a user who last logs in during the final week of the 
cycle may not be a "churned" user but rather a user who stops using the app because their program 
duration ends. Conversely, users who have not logged in for a month before the end of the 
observation window can also start another program, indicating that churn status can be ambiguous 
at the end of fixed observation periods. 
While our results suggest that prediction models can accurately predict who is likely to become 
nonadherent and when, they do not provide insights into the underlying reasons why users 
disengage. Nevertheless, they could serve as valuable research tools, detecting early signs of 
nonadherence and prompting targeted questionnaires to understand disengagement reasons before 
a user is lost to follow-up. This approach could particularly help identifying factors driving 
nonadherence in real-world contexts, where once a user fully disengages, it becomes difficult to 
gather such information [47]. 
It is also important to recognize that adherence to mHealth interventions is an intermediate outcome. 
The primary aim of mHealth interventions is to facilitate health behavior change and ultimately 
improve health outcomes. Although studies suggest a positive association between adherence and 
health outcomes, the link between adherence to mHealth interventions and health outcomes is not 
fully understood and needs further investigation in diverse settings [6]. While evidence from other 
app domains suggests that combining churn prediction models with preventive strategies – such as 
personalized push notifications, omnichannel nudges, or content adaptations – can reduce churn 
[14, 33, 35], it also remains unclear whether this targeted approach can improve adherence and, 
ultimately, health outcomes. Given the relatively new application of churn prediction models in 
mHealth interventions and this study being the first to comprehensively evaluate nonadherence 
prediction models aligned with the definition by Sieverink et al. (2017), significant research gaps 
remain.  
Future research should aim to replicate nonadherence prediction models in diverse mHealth 
contexts and evaluate their integration with targeted preventive strategies in prospective trials to 
assess the impact of these combined approaches on app usage, adherence, and health outcomes.

27 
Addressing these gaps will support the development of more adaptive and impactful mHealth 
interventions and their potential to mitigate the rising prevalence and economic burden of NCDs.
